title: ChronoBox: adaptive timebox arbitration for fair continuous batching and hierarchical KV residency
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem:

Continuous batching delivers throughput but complicates fair access to GPU memory (KV cache) and latency SLOs. Today some multi-tenant workloads monopolize KV residency by holding long-running KV allocations or producing very long sequence requests, which causes other tenants' latency SLOs to slip or triggers large preemptions that hurt end-to-end throughput.

Goal:

Design and implement an adaptive timebox arbitration layer (ChronoBox) that: 1) enforces bounded run-time windows for in-flight batchlets to reduce head-of-line blocking, 2) integrates with hierarchical KV residency tiers (hot/warm/cold) to make preemption decisions mindful of KV residency cost, and 3) coordinates with GPU memory pool reservations so preemption is graceful and predictable. The system must be SLO-aware: prefer small, targeted yields that restore p99 SLOs with minimal regression in throughput and KV hit rate.

Design overview:

- Timebox arbitration: each request entering a continuous batch is assigned a soft timebox determined by tenant SLO profile + observed sequence length distribution. ChronoBox enforces a per-tenant running window (e.g., 50-200ms) after which the batchlet is eligible for yield. This is soft by default (cooperative yield) and hard if GPU pressure or SLO violation risk is high.

- Hierarchical KV residency: KV entries are classified into three tiers: HOT (frequently used, >X hits/min), WARM (recently used), COLD (stale). ChronoBox factors the estimated restore cost of evicting an entry (inference steps/bytes + expected incoming reuse) into preemption decisions. Evicting HOT entries is highly penalized and triggers alternative actions (timebox extension or partial eviction from WARM).

- GPU memory pools: introduce tenant-weighted memory pools (soft reservations) managed by the allocator. ChronoBox can request short-lived burst augmentations or trigger cross-tenant cooperative yielding when pools exceed high-water marks. Pools expose metrics (used, reserved, available, high_water_ts) for decision making.

- Preemption semantics: support three preemption actions with escalating cost: 1) cooperative yield (pause and requeue request to tail of immediate batch), 2) soft preempt (serialize and flush part of KV to WARM tier, continue model with reduced KV), 3) hard preempt (evict KV pages and free memory, terminating in-flight decoding). The scheduler chooses the lightest-weight action that meets SLO pressure constraints.

- SLO feedback loop: ChronoBox consumes per-tenant SLO targets, recent p50/p95/p99 latency drift, and KV hit-rate deltas to adjust timebox sizes and preemption thresholds. There is a decay-based backoff to avoid oscillation across cycles.

Metrics to monitor:
- p99 latency and SLO miss rate (per-tenant, per-model)
- median queueing time and batch formation latency
- KV hit rate by tier and percent of evictions caused by ChronoBox
- GPU memory pool utilization, high-water and reclaim frequency
- throughput (tokens/sec) per-host and per-tenant
- preemption action mix (cooperative/soft/hard)

Rollout plan:

1) Design + unit-tests (this ticket) -> implement ChronoBox controller and APIs for memory pool metrics and KV tiering hooks.
2) Canary: enable ChronoBox in a single Dedicated cluster with low-risk tenants and synthetic workloads exercising long sequences. Observe metrics for 48h.
3) Gradual ramp: enable for ~10% of serving hosts with conservative timeboxes and strict logging.
4) Full: default enablement for tenants with SLOs that opt in or after 2 successful cycles.

Testing strategy:
- Deterministic unit tests for timebox windows, cooperative yield semantics, and TTL decay heuristics.
- Integration bench: replay production traces (long-tail sequences) with KV-access traces to measure p99/regression vs baseline.
- Stress test: multi-tenant load with synthetic hot-set tenants to validate fairness and observe memory reclaiming.
- Chaos test: simulate delayed eviction and kernel OOMs to verify fallback (fallback to smaller model variant or route to dedicated fallback pool).

Trade-offs and risks:
- Tight timeboxes reduce head-of-line blocking but can increase context switching and reduce batching efficiency. We will tune default window sizes per model family to minimize throughput loss (<6% target).
- KV tier classification relies on heuristics; misclassification can increase cold misses. We'll expose parameters as runtime flags and gather telemetry to refine.
- Cooperative yield requires request/resume infrastructure work; if resume isn't available for a model variant, ChronoBox will fall back to preemption policies which may be more disruptive.

Acceptance criteria:

- ChronoBox controller implemented with pluggable policy interface and unit test coverage >= 85% for core paths.
- Metrics emitted and dashboards created for the metrics listed above.
- Canary run shows p99 SLO miss-rate reduction for fairness scenario compared to baseline or <= 10% throughput regression for tenant groups not targeted.
- No production OOMs introduced in canary; KV eviction rate remains within expected bounds.

Deliverables and artifacts:
- Design doc (Confluence) link in links field.
- RFC PR with policy interface and timebox parameters (GitHub link).
- Canary run playbook and dashboard snapshots.

Notes:
- ChronoBox is intentionally conservative at first; default policy: cooperative yield (80ms) -> soft preempt (extra 60ms + partial WARM eviction) -> hard preempt only under severe memory pressure or sustained SLO risk.
acceptance_criteria: ChronoBox controller merged behind feature flag and unit-tested
Telemetry: p99/p95 latency, KV-tier hit rates, memory pool metrics, and preemption action types available in console
Canary run shows ≤10% throughput regression on unaffected tenants and measurable improvement in p99 fairness for overloaded tenants
No new kernel OOM incidents in canary; eviction rate bounded and documented
